title: Working at UPS During 9–11 and After: Looking Back 25 Years Later
author: Joe Allen
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/joeallen1.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/09/11/working-
at-ups-during-9-11-and-after-looking-back-25-years-later/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/joeallen1.png)

9–11 began for me with the phone ringing off the hook. I stumbled to the phone
and listened to my voicemail. It was my mother calling. “Joey, something
terrible has happened. Turn on the TV.” My mother lived in our hometown of
Stoughton, Massachusetts and was watching the morning news programs when it
was announced that the north tower of the World Trade Center (WTC) was hit by
an air plane. It wasn’t clear at first whether this was an accident or not.
But, sixteen minutes later, when the south tower was hit by another plane it
was clear that these weren’t accidents, but a coordinated attack.

My brain wasn’t really working, but I turned on the TV and both towers of the
World Trade Center (WTC) were billowing huge amounts of smoke. It looked like
a[ Hollywood disaster](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/_dBE42j3EzQ) movie. The
Twin Towers were iconic symbols of the New York skyline and used as the
backdrop to countless feature films and television shows. They were familiar
to people around the globe.

I was dead asleep because I worked late at night at UPS in those days. I
started at 6PM on the first part of my “combination full time job” picking up
air packages in my van around the loop, and the second half sorting packages
in the hub at Jeff. St in Chicago. I got home around 2:30 AM and was in bed an
hour later. I almost always shut the ringer off before going to sleep, so my
mother’s call really jarred me.

The carnage and death that day were unprecedented in modern U.S. history. The
speculation during the days that followed was that potentially up to 10,000
people could have been killed and untold missing. (The[ final list of
victims](https://www.911memorial.org/visit/memorial/names-911-memorial) from
the Twin Towers was 2,977. )[ Frantic last
calls](https://www.history.com/articles/september-11-attacks-final-phone-
calls) were made by passengers on highjacked planes and from the Twin Towers.
In many cases they could only leave messages on answering machine. After the
towers collapsed,[ cell
phones](https://www.si.edu/collections/snapshot/911-cell-phone), the internet,
and landlines were down, which made contacting friends and family impossible.

Watching the towers collapse is the worst thing I ever witnessed. The thought
of people dyeing in the violent impact of the two planes, collapsing floors
and concrete, or burned to death with jet fuel was horrifying. We only learned
later of the terrible fate of the fireman who entered the towers to rescue
those injured or trapped in their offices many dozens of stories above the
streets. I was pretty much glued to the TV for the rest of the day, while
talking frantically to friends speculating in panic mode about what was going
to happen next.

President George W. Bush[ declared](https://georgewbush-
whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2001/09/20010914-4.html) a national
emergency. It wasn’t clear if this was the first and only wave of attacks, or
there were more to come. All civilian aircraft was grounded and fighter jets
were deployed to the skies for the first time since WWII. Bush was[
shuttled](https://www.whitehousehistory.org/photos/fotoware?id=6052da61-c33a-4d96-8209-cb3bb90b7669)
around the country until he returned to Washington, DC. and[
addressed](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gz7S1v1k664) the nation that
evening from the oval office. News accounts reported that all government
buildings and private businesses were sending everyone home. The streets were
soon empty.

Despite Bush’s declaration, UPS declared that they were still working. UPS
said something idiotic like they weren’t going to let the terrorists stop
them. Once again, demonstrating what a money-grubbing, big cult UPS is. I
called into the air department sometime in the late afternoon, and after they
made a halfhearted attempt to get me to come in, I said, “If you think I’m
coming in to work tonight, you’re out of your mind.”

Since all civilian aircraft would be grounded for the next week, there were
going to be no Next Day Air (NDA) deliveries. The idea of going from one
closed office building to another in the Loop filled with skyscrapers just
seemed bizarre to me. While I was no longer doing pickups throughout the Sears
Tower, I couldn’t help but think about what it would have been like to have
been trapped in there if the attacks occurred in Chicago and not New York. My
old friend, and former UPSer, Danny Katch[
wrote](https://jacobin.com/2020/05/coronavirus-covid-911-september11-attacks-
ground-zero) about his experince of surviving the 9–11 attacks in lower
Manhattan. Danny’s UPS supervisor demanded that they stay in place. “If you
leave, turn over your ID, because you’re not coming back.” They left.

The next day I went to work. I can’t remember if we did our routes or just
sorted in the hub, but I do remember that UPS wanted to go through with a some
kind of pie eating contest for part timers. UPS engaged in alll sorts of
“company spirit” antics to keep part-timers on the jobs. I remember being
enraged and yelling at one supervisor, “What’s wrong with you people? There
might be 10,000 people dead in New York, and you want to do this?” He looked
at me like I was crazy. I took the issues of war and their consequences very
personally.

I remember walking around for days feeling like there was a brick on my head
and a cannonball in my stomach. Everyone knew that war was coming. Most of my
coworkers were more bewildered by events than bloodthirsty. Bush wasn’t very
popular with many Black and Latino working class people, and in large parts of
the labor movement. He was declared the winner in the 2000 presidential
election by the Supreme Court despite the suppression of Black votes in
Florida. Bush “won” the election with a minority of popular vote against Al
Gore, the sitting vice-president, and viewed as illegitimate by large parts of
the electorate, as Trump would be 2016. Bush was[ anti-
union](https://www.counterpunch.org/2002/10/18/bush-and-bosses-target-
dockworkers/)and appointed all sorts of neo-conservatives to his cabinet.
Before Trump, Bush was seen as one of the most anti-working class presidents
in U.S. history, on par with Ronald Reagan.

Yet, despite Bush’s unpopularity with many people before 9–11, the crisis
suddenly gave him the cache of now being a “war-time” president. The
population rallied around the president helped by the mainstream media, and
the anti-Arab and anti-Muslim racism and bigotry already embraced by large
numbers of Americans. Xenophobia and racism skyrocketed over the next year. It
was impossible to have rational discussions about the “blowback” of U.S.
foreign policy while the hunt for Osama Bin-Laden and Al-Quieda was on.
Antiwar activism was marginal to irrelevant. It was only when Bush’s war
planner shifted towards Iraq that antiwar began to resurface.

**Teamsters 705 on Chicago**

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-08-at-4.35.08-PM-680x874.png)

Over the next year and a half, those of us in the International Socialist
Organization (ISO), which I was a member of for four decades, and worked at
UPS and active in the Teamsters talked about how to respond to the events. The
U.S. soon after 9–11 invaded and occupied Afghanistan and began to prepare to
invade Iraq, which seemed to be the whole point of the “Global War on Terror.”
UPS eventually made a ton of money off the war. UPS had close ties to the
Republican Party and the Bush administration. Bush was also aided by Teamster
General James P. Hoffa, who joined the infamous[Committee for the Liberation
of Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Committee_for_the_Liberation_of_Iraq),
to lobby for the invasion of Iraq.

In Chicago, a small but important labor against the war campaign was coming
together. I took these issues very seriously.[
Vietnam](https://tempestmag.org/2022/03/stoughtons-forever-war/) cast a long
shadow over my family. I am proud to say that the ISO played a pretty
important role in this. We were aided in this by the late[ Bill
Davis](https://vn-agentorange.org/bill-davis-president-of-vvaw-and-vaoorc-
board-member-1948-2007/), a long standing member of Vietnam Veterans against
the War (VVAW), who was the working president of the machinists local that
represented mechanics at UPS in Chicago. When President George Bush[
visited](https://georgewbush-
whitehouse.archives.gov/news/releases/2002/05/20020513-6.html) our UPS hub at
Jeff St. in late Spring of 2002, to tout some welfare reform scam that UPS was
milking — me, Leighton, and Donny leafleted (along with my late friend Dave
Healy) to package drivers coming into work with a flier attacking Bush’s
record. We didn’t catch any shit from anyone.

While we didn’t get any shit from our coworkers, I got more calls from the
union hall not to do it, than I ever did from them to do something against
UPS. Later at the Teamsters 705 membership meeting, the Secretary-Treasurer at
the time, the late[ Jerry
Zero](https://socialistworker.org/2017/05/03/a-fighter-against-the-teamsters-
old-guard), whom I personally liked but was increasingly frustrated with, read
large parts of the leaflet to the audience. He gave the strong impression that
it was his idea. Oh, well, that’s politics. Later in October 2002, UPS part-
timer Kieran Knutson, introduced the
now[famous](https://inthesetimes.com/article/unions-against-the-war)
resolution against the Iraq War at the membership meeting. It passed
overwhelmingly. It was later[
included](https://www.howardzinn.org/collection/voices-of-a-peoples-history-
book/) in Howard Zinn’s _Voices of a People’s History of the United States_.

Teamsters 705, which at the time was the second largest Teamsters local union
in the country, would soon host two important meetings for the future of labor
antiwar activism in the coming years. On January 10, 2003, _Voices Against the
War: Union Activists and Veterans Speak Out Against the War Drive on Iraq_.
The speakers included Bill Davis, a leader in[ _Vietnam Veteran against the
War_](https://www.vvaw.org/gallery/Bill_Davis.php) and a shop steward for the
machinists union at UPS, and Dane Lane, also a Vietnam Veteran, who became
well know as a “Road Warrior” during the Staley Lockout in the mid-1990s. The
panel was round out by Trent Willis, a representative of west coast
International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILGWU) and Brenda Stokeley, an
AFCSME president from New York and a co-covenor New York City Labor against
the War. The meeting led to the formation of Chicago Labor Against the War
(CLAW).

The following day on January 11, Teamsters 705 hosted the founding convention
of[ U.S. Labor against the
War.](https://www.counterpunch.org/2003/01/17/workers-against-war/) It was the
most significant anti-war formation since the latter years of the Vietnam War.
When the first Teamster died in Iraq, we publicized it with a mass fliering at
Jeff St. His parents were active members of[ Military Families against the
War](https://www.democracynow.org/2004/5/13/parents_of_u_s_soldier_killed).

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-08-at-4.33.14-PM-680x876.png)

The years following 9–11 were some of the most trying times I’ve ever lived
through. I was proud of the work the ISO did in those years which couldn’t
have been done without our friends and allies like Bill Davis, Dan Lane, and
Kieran Knutson, who has remained active in the Twin Cities’ labor movement as
a Local CWA president and in the[
resistance](https://inequality.org/article/labors-role-in-minnesotas-ice-
resistance/) to ICE. Eventually antiwar sentiment made it all the way up to
the leaders of the AFL-CIO. In June 2005, the AFL-CIO passed a[
resolution](https://aflcio.org/resolutions/resolution-50-war-not-answer) that
called for the “rapid withdrawal” of U.S. forces from Iraq. If you told me in
the days after 9–11 that that was going to happen, I would have thought you
were nuts. It goes to show how quickly things can change.

Later](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/09/11/working-at-ups-during-9-11-and-
